implementation_notes: ReSwift is the explicit Redux port for Swift ('Unidirectional Data Flow in Swift - Inspired by Redux'): a Store<AppState> is created from a reducer function of type (Action, AppState?) -> AppState, subscribers register with store.subscribe(self) and receive the new state through newState(state:), middleware wraps dispatch, and select(subState) lets a subscriber receive only a mapped slice - which ReSwift skips notifying when the slice is Equatable and unchanged. The state is a value-type struct tree, so immutability is partly structural, but the store is still hand-fed: what replaces the classic structure is the library's store/reducer pair; use it when one app-wide state graph with middleware and logging is genuinely required, and prefer the Observation variant for ordinary SwiftUI state.
pitfalls: The reducer must return a value-type state: a class instance inside AppState mutates the previously published snapshot and defeats equality-based subscription.
Subscribers registered with subscribe(self) must unsubscribe in deinit/onDisappear or the store keeps view controllers alive and updates dead views.
Dispatching from inside a reducer or from middleware that re-dispatches the same action type creates loops; ReSwift asserts only some of these in debug builds.
selecting a sub-state relies on Equatable and a deterministic mapping - a closure returning fresh non-equatable values notifies on every change.

variants.name: SwiftUI Observation: @Observable model injected through the environment
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftUI's own data flow replaces the store for most applications: an @Observable class (Observation framework, Swift 5.9+) holds the shared state, views track exactly the properties their body reads, mutations are ordinary property assignments made from intents, and one model injected with .environment(...)/@Environment acts as the application-scoped source of truth while @State stays for view-local state. This is the idiomatic alternative to a hand-rolled Flux layer - it keeps the one-way spirit (views read, intents mutate) without a dispatcher, reducers or action types - and the classic Redux structure is justified only when you need the audit log, middleware or time travel that observation alone does not provide.
pitfalls: Mutating an @Observable model off the main actor interleaves UI updates; mark the model @MainActor or marshal mutations to the main thread.
Observation tracks the properties a view body actually reads, so values derived outside the body do not trigger updates - derive inside the view or publish the derived value.
A model stored in @State per view is not global: two roots create two models, so app-wide state needs the single instance at the App/Scene level.
Passing an @Observable object as a plain (non-@Bindable) parameter gives read-only access; two-way edits to a property need @Bindable or an explicit binding, otherwise intents silently do nothing.
